r0.why: Fine-grained, no obvious compositional layering, splits into thin slabs and plates [12]; usually low-grade regional metamorphism of mudrock [13].

r1.why: Foliation called slaty cleavage, caused by strong compression with clay flakes regrowing perpendicular [4]; may not match sedimentary layering [3]; independent of sedimentary structures, reflects regional compression [16].

r2.why: Up to 50% volume loss on compaction [22], platy grains rotated into perpendicular layers starting cleavage [23], fully developed as clay converts to chlorite and mica [24], carbon to graphite [25].

r3.why: Mild metamorphism, microscopic crystals, dull fresh surfaces [14]; silky phyllite next grade [15]; planes too close for hand sample [17]; quartz-feldspar lenses and mica layers under 100 um [19][20].

r4.why: All three statements are in [21]: low heat and pressure relative to most metamorphic rocks, hence some fossils, sometimes microscopic delicate remains.

r5.why: Fissility, smooth flat sheets, roofing/floor tiles/billiard tables [5]; water absorption under 0.4% and frost resistance, roofing suitability [42]; lasts several hundred years with little maintenance [45].

r6.why: Writing slate small, smooth, often wood-framed, used with chalk, pub charges [10]; origin of clean/blank slate phrases [11].
